    Kong Xiong v. Attorney General United States of America (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-25-03366 / USCOURTS-ca3-25-03366-0

    FAPD-AI: The Third Circuit's nonprecedential per curiam opinion filed November 5, 2026 in Kong Meng Xiong v. Attorney General (No. 25-3366) grants Xiong's petition for review of a Board of Immigration Appeals order that summarily dismissed his appeal as untimely. The court concluded that the EOIR letter mailed September 10, 2025 described the decision as the written decision and stated a 30-day appeal deadline from mailing, and that the Board received Xiong's notice of appeal on October 9, 2025, so the appeal should have been deemed timely filed. The court remanded the case for the Board to consider the substance of the appeal. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:21:47 Eastern time ET
    Joseph Pilchesky v. Office of Attorney General Pennsylvania, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-26-01642 / USCOURTS-ca3-26-01642-0

    FAPD-AI: On November 5, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit issued a non-precedential per curiam opinion affirming the Middle District of Pennsylvania's dismissal of pro se appellant Joseph Pilchesky's amended complaint against the Pennsylvania Office of the Attorney General and several of its officials. The court held that the Office and the officials in their official capacities were immune under the Eleventh Amendment, that Deputy Attorneys General McCarthy and Mahler were entitled to prosecutorial immunity on the individual-capacity claims, and that the remaining issues were forfeited or unsupported by the record. The court also found that the District Court had independently reviewed the Magistrate Judge's report before adopting it. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:21:47 Eastern time ET
    Abrahim Fata v. Edwin Arcelly, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-26-02661 / USCOURTS-ca3-26-02661-0

    FAPD-AI: On November 5, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit issued a non-precedential per curiam opinion affirming the Eastern District of Pennsylvania's screening dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) of pro se appellant Abrahim Fata's complaint. The court held that Fata did not plead the elements of a RICO claim or a TVPA forced-labor claim, did not state an equal protection class-of-one claim, and did not identify a protected liberty interest supporting a procedural due process claim. The court further held that leave to amend would be futile. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:21:46 Eastern time ET
    GEA Mechanical Equipment US Inc v. First State Insurance Co, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-25-02395 / USCOURTS-ca3-25-02395-0

    FAPD-AI: The Third Circuit's nonprecedential opinion filed November 5, 2026 in GEA Mechanical Equipment US, Inc. v. First State Insurance Co. (No. 25-2395) vacates the District of New Jersey's summary judgment order in favor of the insurers on a late-notice defense and remands the case for further proceedings. The court concluded that under New Jersey law the insurer had not met its burden of showing appreciable prejudice, because it had not shown a likelihood of achieving a better settlement result. The court states that the disposition is not an opinion of the full court and is not binding precedent under I.O.P. 5.7. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:21:45 Eastern time ET
    In re: Tiger (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-26-03220 / USCOURTS-ca10-26-03220-0

    FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit's November 5, 2026 order in In re: Tiger (No. 26-3220) denies Pidy T. Tiger's motion for authorization to file a second or successive 28 U.S.C. § 2254 habeas petition. The court found that the third claim did not meet the due diligence requirement of 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)(B)(i), because Tiger raised the underlying issue on direct appeal before filing his first petition, and that his first and second claims, even if proven, would not meet the standard of § 2244(b)(2)(B)(ii). Under § 2244(b)(3)(E), the denial is not appealable and is not subject to rehearing or certiorari. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:21:45 Eastern time ET
    Williams v. City of Gillette, Wyoming, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-26-08001 / USCOURTS-ca10-26-08001-0

    FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit's November 5, 2026 order and judgment in Williams v. City of Gillette, Wyoming, et al. (No. 26-8001) affirms the District of Wyoming's dismissal of pro se plaintiff Bruce Williams's civil rights complaint against the City of Gillette and its mayor. The court held that claims based on the Wyoming Constitution or Wyoming state law are not cognizable under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and affirmed their dismissal with prejudice, and it affirmed the dismissal of claims based on violations occurring more than four years before suit, the applicable limitations period in Wyoming. The order and judgment is not binding precedent, except under the doctrines of law of the case, res judicata, and collateral estoppel. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:21:44 Eastern time ET
    Jensen v. Bank of New York Mellon, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-25-01430 / USCOURTS-ca10-25-01430-0

    FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit affirmed a district court order that upheld a bankruptcy court ruling allowing Bank of New York Mellon's proof of claim on real property owned by the appellant, Linn W. Jensen, and overruled her statute-of-limitations objection. Applying Colorado law, the court held that the lender's withdrawal of notices of election and demand for sale in 2011, 2013, and 2015 manifested abandonment of acceleration, which restored the note's original maturity date for limitations purposes. The court also treated the appellant's undeveloped challenge to a Zoom-conducted bankruptcy trial as waived. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit granted defense counsel's Anders motion to withdraw and dismissed the appeal of Jacob Daniel Lickers from a six-month prison sentence and reimposed lifetime supervised release following revocation of supervised release. Counsel's brief identified four potential issues, including the facts underlying the violation, the revocation hearing, the reasonableness of the sentence, and the lifetime supervised release term. The court reviewed the record and concluded that none of the issues was nonfrivolous. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:21:43 Eastern time ET
    United States v. Morgan (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-24-03186 / USCOURTS-ca10-24-03186-0

    FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the convictions of Brett Morgan, entered by a jury in the District of Kansas, on three counts of production of child pornography, six counts of attempted production, and one count of possession, along with the eighty-year prison term imposed. The case involved secretly recorded images of five minors in the defendant's care. The opinion, designated for publication, addressed the meaning of lascivious exhibition under 18 U.S.C. § 2256(2)(A)(v), agreed with the government's position on that standard, and rejected the defendant's other challenges. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:21:40 Eastern time ET
    United States v. Bindues (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-24-02117 / USCOURTS-ca10-24-02117-0

    FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the convictions of Johnathon Bindues, a former high school athletic coach, for coercing and enticing a fourteen-year-old to engage in sexual activity under 18 U.S.C. § 2422(b) and for enticing the minor to produce child pornography under 18 U.S.C. § 2251. The District of New Mexico had imposed a 276-month prison term and ten years of supervised release. The appellate court held that the record contained sufficient evidence to support the § 2251 conviction and that the district court did not abuse its discretion in admitting the government's expert testimony. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit denied the petition for review by Juan Linares-Recendiz of a Board of Immigration Appeals decision that reversed an immigration judge's grant of cancellation of removal.     Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-25-02756 / USCOURTS-ca7-25-02756-0

    FAPD-AI: This nonprecedential order, filed under docket No. 25-2756 with the companion appeal No. 25-2522, contains the same text as the order in that appeal and affirms the conviction and 120-month sentence of Joseph Perkins for attempted enticement of a minor under 18 U.S.C. § 2422(b).     Deandre Cherry v. USA (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-21-02231 / USCOURTS-ca7-21-02231-0

    FAPD-AI: In this opinion, decided November 5, 2026, the Seventh Circuit considered DeAndre Cherry's motion under 28 U.S.C. § 2255, which raised ineffective-assistance-of-counsel claims under Strickland v. Washington regarding sentencing enhancements and the testimony of Special Agent David Brazao. The court held that counsel's failure to object to the statutory enhancement under 21 U.S.C. § 841(b)(1)(B) prejudiced Cherry, but that the career-offender claim was foreclosed by United States v. Ruth and the testimony claim did not prejudice the defense. The court vacated the sentence and remanded for resentencing. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:04:45 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Joseph Perkins (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-25-02522 / USCOURTS-ca7-25-02522-0

    FAPD-AI: In this nonprecedential order, the Seventh Circuit affirmed a 120-month sentence imposed on Joseph Perkins after a jury convicted him of attempted enticement of a minor under 18 U.S.C. § 2422(b). Perkins had contended that the district judge should have given the jury an entrapment instruction, and the panel agreed with the district judge that the evidence did not support either governmental inducement or lack of predisposition. The order states that the sexual messages were initiated and repeated by Perkins, and that the FBI agent's posing account's communications were innocent in nature. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    USA v. Jamill McDonald (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-25-03344 / USCOURTS-ca6-25-03344-0

    FAPD-AI: In this per curiam opinion, not recommended for publication, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed the drug convictions of Jamill McDonald, who had argued that his trial violated the Speedy Trial Act and that evidence from a search of his apartment should have been suppressed. The opinion recounts that officers responding to a reported burglary found a brick of cocaine in plain view during a safety sweep, after which they obtained a warrant and recovered additional narcotics, cash, scales, and phones. The court rejected both challenges and affirmed the judgment, and Judge Hermandorfer filed a separate opinion concurring in part and concurring in the judgment. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Text of Senate Amendment 1124 (opens in a new tab)
    Congressional Record · govinfo API · CREC-2021-03-05 / CREC-2021-03-05-pt1-PgS1314-5

    FAPD-AI: Senate amendment SA 1124, submitted by Mr. Lee on March 5, 2021, proposes to strike section 9901 of H.R. 1319 and insert a new provision adding section 602 to Title VI of the Social Security Act, which establishes a Coronavirus State Fiscal Recovery Fund. The text appropriates $219.8 billion for fiscal year 2021 for payments to states, territories, and Tribal governments, reserving $4.5 billion for territories, $20 billion for Tribal governments, and $195.3 billion for the 50 states and the District of Columbia, along with allocation formulas and a $50 million administrative appropriation. The amendment limits permitted uses of funds, bars use of funds to offset tax reductions or for pension fund deposits, and sets certification, reporting, and recoupment requirements; the source text is truncated before its regulations provision. CREC-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: SA 1833, submitted by Senator Scott for himself and Senator Portman, would strike section 13823 of H.R. 1 and insert a new subchapter Z, 'Opportunity Zones,' into chapter 1 of the Internal Revenue Code. The inserted text describes how governors nominate low-income census tracts for designation as qualified opportunity zones, caps designations at 25 percent of a state's low-income communities, and permits contiguous tracts with median family income up to 125 percent of the adjacent low-income community's. It also provides an election to defer capital gains invested in qualified opportunity funds, with basis adjustments for investments held 5, 7, and 10 years, and the source text is truncated. CREC-SEL-01

    Congressional Record · govinfo API · CREC-2019-05-23 / CREC-2019-05-23-pt1-PgS3073

    FAPD-AI: Senators Wicker, Markey, and Thune spoke on the Senate floor about S. 151, the Telephone Robocall Abuse Criminal Enforcement and Deterrence Act (TRACED Act), before its final passage vote. Wicker stated that the bill would give the FCC tools to address robocall violators, require phone companies to authenticate calls, and involve the Attorney General in prosecuting robocall violations. Markey cited an estimated 48 billion robocalls received by consumers in 2018 and described the bill's three elements as call authentication, call blocking, and extending the FCC's penalty window from 1 year to 3 years.     Telephone Robocall Abuse Criminal Enforcement and Deterrence Act (opens in a new tab)
    Congressional Record · govinfo API · CREC-2019-05-23 / CREC-2019-05-23-pt1-PgS3075-2

    FAPD-AI: The Senate considered S. 151 with a committee amendment that would amend Section 227 of the Communications Act of 1934 to add civil forfeiture penalties for robocall violations, including an additional penalty of up to $10,000 for violations committed with intent. The text sets limitation periods of 1 year for general violations and 3 years for intentional violations, requires an annual FCC report to Congress on robocall and spoofed-call enforcement, and requires providers to implement the STIR/SHAKEN call authentication framework within 18 months of enactment unless the FCC makes specified determinations. The excerpt is truncated before the full text of the remaining sections, including the rulemaking on unauthenticated numbers and the safe harbor provisions, is shown. CREC-SEL-01

    The Arctic (opens in a new tab)
    Congressional Record · govinfo API · CREC-2019-05-23 / CREC-2019-05-23-pt1-PgS3079-2

    FAPD-AI: Senator Murkowski's floor statement addresses Arctic policy, including the Arctic Council Ministerial Meeting held May 6 and 7, 2019, in Rovaniemi, Finland, which ended without a signed ministerial declaration but with a joint ministerial statement by all eight Arctic nations reaffirming cooperation, sustainable development, and the rights of indigenous peoples. The statement describes U.S. icebreaker capacity, including a contract awarded for the design and construction of a polar-class icebreaker and $20 million provided for long-lead materials for a second polar security cutter. It also summarizes remarks by Secretary of State Pompeo on Russian and Chinese activity in the Arctic and notes that the Arctic Council was established in 1996 with military and national security issues excluded from its activities.     FAPD-AI: The Senate agreed to the motion to proceed to H.R. 2157, a supplemental appropriations act for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2019, and adopted Amendment No. 250, a Shelby-Leahy substitute. Senator Leahy's statement describes provisions including $19.1 billion to help communities in listed States and territories rebuild, $605 million for the Nutrition Assistance Program in Puerto Rico, and a separate $4.5 billion presidential request for southern border humanitarian assistance that the statement describes as still under negotiation.     FAPD-AI: Senate amendment SA 250, proposed by Senator McConnell for Senator Shelby and Senator Leahy, would strike all text after the enacting clause of H.R. 2157, a supplemental appropriations bill for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2019, and insert new provisions. The amendment provides appropriations for agricultural and disaster-related programs, including $3,005,442,000 for the Office of the Secretary for crop and tree losses, $480,000,000 for the Emergency Forest Restoration Program, $558,000,000 for the Emergency Conservation Program, $435,000,000 for watershed and flood prevention operations, and $150,000,000 for rural community facilities grants. Section 103 makes persons or legal entities with average adjusted gross income above $900,000 ineligible for Market Facilitation Program payments, unless at least 75 percent of their adjusted gross income is derived from farming, ranching, or forestry related activities.     FAPD-AI: The Senate Record of March 5, 2021 prints SA 1031, proposed by Senator Lankford and Senator Daines, which would strike section 2204 through the end of subtitle H of title II of H.R. 1319 and insert new provisions. The inserted text appropriates funds under the Family Violence Prevention and Services Act, including $198,000,000 for grants supporting survivors of sexual assault and $49,500,000 for grants to culturally specific populations, and adds sections 2205 and 2206 providing $250,000,000 and $100,000,000 for child abuse prevention and treatment and $852,000,000 for the Corporation for National and Community Service. The amendment also adds section 2301 relating to the Public Health Service Act, and the text is truncated in the source. CREC-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: Ms. Collins and cosponsors proposed amendment SA 1242 to amendment SA 891 to H.R. 1319 as a substitute in lieu of the matter to be inserted. Its table of contents reduces Title IV to three sections, covering public health programs (Sec. 4001), schools (Sec. 4101), and child care (Sec. 4201), while retaining the agriculture, finance, small business, and homeland security titles. The Title I text matches the SNAP, WIC, and nutrition provisions described in SA 1151, including the SNAP benefit extension to September 30, 2021, $1.15 billion for SNAP administrative expenses, and a WIC cash-value voucher increase up to $35 with $490 million, and the excerpt is truncated in the source.     FAPD-AI: Mr. Rubio submitted amendment SA 1296, intended to be proposed to amendment SA 891 to H.R. 1319 and ordered to lie on the table, which would add a section titled Medical Manufacturing Economic Development and Sustainability at the end of subtitle G of title IX. The proposed Internal Revenue Code Subchapter AA would allow a credit of 40 percent (60 percent for qualified repatriated pharmaceutical manufacturing facilities) of certain wages, employee fringe benefit expenses, and depreciation for medical product manufacturing facilities in economically distressed zones, and a credit of 30 percent (5 percent for related persons) for qualified products and services acquired from those zones. The provision also allows an election to expense certain facility property and defines economically distressed zones as census tracts with a poverty rate of at least 35 percent for each of the five most recent calendar years or meeting alternative criteria, and the excerpt is truncated in the source.     FAPD-AI: Senate amendment SA 1313, submitted by Ms. Murkowski to amendment SA 891 to H.R. 1319, would strike section 9901 and insert a new Title VI provision of the Social Security Act establishing a Coronavirus State Fiscal Recovery Fund. It appropriates $219,300,000,000 for fiscal year 2021, available through December 31, 2024, for payments to States, territories, and Tribal governments, plus $50,000,000 for administrative costs. The text reserves $4,500,000,000 for territories, $19,500,000,000 for Tribal governments, and $195,300,000,000 for the 50 States and the District of Columbia, and restricts use of the funds, including prohibiting deposits into pension funds.     FAPD-AI: Senate amendment SA 1336, submitted by Mr. Moran to amendment SA 891 to H.R. 1319, proposes replacing section 2 with a table of contents and inserting provisions under Title I (Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions), Title II (Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs), and Title III (Committee on Finance). The Title I provisions appropriate $7,500,000,000 to the CDC for COVID-19 vaccine activities, $1,000,000,000 for vaccine confidence activities, $6,050,000,000 for vaccine supply chain activities, $500,000,000 for FDA activities, and $47,800,000,000 for COVID-19 testing, contact tracing, and mitigation. The amendment also amends the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act to treat individuals receiving unemployment compensation during 2021 as meeting certain requirements and to disregard household income above 133 percent of the poverty line for that purpose.     FAPD-AI: Senate amendment SA 1339, submitted by Mr. Rubio and Mr. Lee to amendment SA 891 to H.R. 1319, would strike part 2 of subtitle G of title IX and insert Child Tax Credit provisions for 2021. The text amends Internal Revenue Code section 24 to set the credit at $3,500 per qualifying child ($4,500 for children under age 6), treat 17-year-olds as qualifying children, and reduce the credit by $50 for each $1,000 of modified adjusted gross income above $150,000 for joint returns, $112,500 for heads of household, and $75,000 for other filers. It also adds Internal Revenue Code section 7527A, directing the Secretary to establish periodic advance payments of the credit and an online portal for electing out of payments and updating eligibility information. CREC-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: Senate amendment SA 1362, submitted by Mr. Romney to amendment SA 891 to H.R. 1319, would strike subtitle M of title IX and insert a Coronavirus State and Local Fiscal Recovery Funds provision adding section 602 to Title VI of the Social Security Act. It appropriates $125,600,000,000 for fiscal year 2021, available through December 31, 2024, with reserved amounts of $2,571,428,571 for territories, $11,428,571,429 for Tribal governments, and $111,600,000,000 for the 50 States and the District of Columbia, plus $50,000,000 for administration. The text limits use of the funds to COVID-19 response, government services to the extent of revenue reductions, and water, sewer, or broadband investments, and prohibits using the funds to offset tax reductions or for deposit into pension funds. CREC-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: Senate amendment SA 1378, proposed by Mr. Wyden to amendment SA 891 to H.R. 1319, would strike part 1 of subtitle A of title IX and insert Crisis Support for Unemployed Workers provisions. It extends CARES Act pandemic unemployment provisions to weeks ending on or before September 6, 2021, including increasing the maximum number of Pandemic Unemployment Assistance weeks from 50 to 79 and Pandemic Emergency Unemployment Compensation weeks from 24 to 53. Part 3 of the amendment appropriates $8,000,000 for Department of Labor administration and $2,000,000,000 for fraud prevention, equitable access, and timely payment under a new CARES Act section 2118.     FAPD-AI: Senate amendment SA 1380, submitted by Mr. Lee and Mr. Rubio to amendment SA 891 to H.R. 1319, would strike part 2 of subtitle G of title IX through the end of part 4 and insert Child Tax Credit provisions for 2021. This version sets the credit at $3,300 per qualifying child ($4,100 for children under age 6), with the same age, income phaseout, and $50-per-$1,000 reduction provisions as amendment SA 1339.     FAPD-AI: Amendment SA 1381, proposed by Lee and Rubio to amendment SA 891 to H.R. 1319, would strike parts 2 through 4 of subtitle G of title IX and insert a new Part 2 on the child tax credit. The inserted text adds special rules for 2021 taxable years to Section 24 of the Internal Revenue Code, including a $3,300 credit amount ($4,200 for children under age 6), a reduction based on modified adjusted gross income with threshold amounts of $150,000, $112,500, and $75,000, and treatment of 17-year-olds as qualifying children. It also adds Section 7527A, which directs the Secretary to establish periodic advance payments of the credit and an online portal for electing out of payments and submitting updated information.     FAPD-AI: Amendment SA 1398, proposed by Schumer to amendment SA 891 to H.R. 1319, revises that amendment by setting minimum funding percentages for listed purposes, reducing a dollar figure on page 33 from $125,804,800,000 to $122,774,800,000, and adding Section 2014 to appropriate $2,580,000,000 for part B grants, $200,000,000 for preschool grants, and $250,000,000 for infants and toddlers under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act. It also amends the Railroad Unemployment Insurance Act and Section 2112 of the CARES Act to replace the March 14, 2021 dates with September 6, 2021, and extends certain railroad unemployment benefit durations. The amendment further adds Section 4015, which deems covered Federal employees diagnosed with COVID-19 between January 27, 2020 and January 27, 2023 to have an injury caused by exposure to the novel coronavirus for workers' compensation claims under subchapter I of chapter 81 of title 5, United States Code, excluding employees who are exclusively teleworking during a covered exposure period.     official summary: We, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Service), announce technical corrections for 43 wildlife and plant species under the Endangered Species Act of 1973, as amended (Act). For 7 wildlife species and 30 plant species that predominately occur in California and Nevada, we are revising the List of Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and the List of Endangered and Threatened Plants (“the Lists”) to reflect the current scientifically accepted taxonomy and nomenclature of these species. We are also making commensurate revisions to the applicable critical habitat sections. Further, for six wildlife species occurring within the United States and territories, we are correcting errors in the Lists made in previous publications.     official summary: This final rule with comment period revises the Medicare Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS) and the Medicare Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC) payment system for calendar year 2027 based on our continuing experience with these systems.     official summary: The Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission” or the “SEC”) is amending the definitions of “small business” and “small organization” (collectively, “small entities”) that are used in connection with Commission rulemaking under the Investment Company Act of 1940 (the “Investment Company Act”) and the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 (the “Advisers Act”). These definitions concern regulatory requirements applicable to registered investment companies and business development companies (collectively, “funds”) as well as investment advisers. The definitions are used specifically for purposes of the Regulatory Flexibility Act (the “RFA”), which requires the Commission to consider the impact of its regulations on small entities. The amendments are designed to modernize the definitions, by increasing certain asset-based thresholds, including a mechanism for periodic future inflation adjustments, and eliminating the threshold based on total assets for advisers.     Anti-Communism Week, 2026 (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · FR-2026-11-06 / 2026-22787

    FAPD-AI: Proclamation 11078, dated November 3, 2026, designates the week of November 1 through November 7, 2026 as Anti-Communism Week. The proclamation describes communist and socialist ideologies as threats to individual liberty, and it references the effects of state control over thought, creativity, and political expression. It calls on Americans to defend the Constitution and the nation's founding principles against those ideologies during the observance. FR-SEL-03

    The American Declaration of Freedom in Space (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · FR-2026-11-06 / 2026-22789

    FAPD-AI: Proclamation 11079, dated November 3, 2026, is titled "The American Declaration of Freedom in Space." It proclaims that the solar system and all of outer space beyond Earth are open to exploration, development, use, and the establishment of a permanent presence by American citizens, consistent with United States law and the country's international obligations. The document also references the Artemis II mission's April flight around the Moon, the planned Artemis III test campaign next summer, and a goal of returning to the Moon by 2028. FR-SEL-03

    119 HR 3100 RH: Comprehensive Health and Integrity in Licensing and Documentation Act of 2026 (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr3100rh

    FAPD-AI: The reported bill, titled the Comprehensive Health and Integrity in Licensing and Documentation Act of 2026 (CHILD Act of 2026), amends Section 5(9)(B) of the National Child Protection Act of 1993 to expand the definition of covered individual. The amended definition would include persons employed by, contracting with, or volunteering with an entity under contract with a qualified entity, as well as persons who are or seek to be licensed or certified by a qualified entity. The bill was reported with an amendment and committed to the Committee of the Whole House on November 5, 2026. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 00:01:27 Eastern time ET
    119 HR 3978 RH: Nuclear REFUEL (Recycling Efficient Fuels Utilizing Expedited Licensing) Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr3978rh

    FAPD-AI: The reported bill, the Nuclear REFUEL (Recycling Efficient Fuels Utilizing Expedited Licensing) Act, amends the definition of production facility in Section 11 v. of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954. The amendment adds reprocessing of spent nuclear fuel in a manner that does not isolate plutonium to the activities listed in that definition, and it inserts the word reprocessing into the existing text on uranium enrichment. The bill was reported with an amendment and committed to the Committee of the Whole House on November 5, 2026. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 00:01:27 Eastern time ET
    119 HR 5549 RH: Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr5549rh

    FAPD-AI: The bill, titled the Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act, amends the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 to change hearing procedures for nuclear facility licensing. It allows the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to issue construction permits, operating licenses, and related amendments without a hearing when no affected person requests one, after thirty days notice and Federal Register publication. The bill also requires informal adjudicatory procedures for any hearing held, conditions uranium enrichment facility hearings on a request from an affected person, and applies to pending applications on enactment. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 00:01:27 Eastern time ET
    119 HR 5723 RH: Fraud Reduction And Uncovering Deception in VA Disability Exams Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr5723rh

    FAPD-AI: The reported bill, the Fraud Reduction And Uncovering Deception in VA Disability Exams Act (FRAUD in VA Disability Exams Act), adds Section 5322 to chapter 53 of title 38, United States Code. That section directs the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to identify fraud in disability benefit questionnaire forms, establish a process for claims processors to report suspected fraud to the Office of Inspector General, direct routine audits, and inform claimants when information is insufficient to assign a rating, with an annual report to the Veterans' Affairs committees. The bill also amends Section 312 of title 38 to authorize the Inspector General to deposit funds from undercover investigations in designated accounts or financial institutions, requires quarterly audits and an annual report by November 30, and takes effect 90 days after enactment. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 00:01:27 Eastern time ET
    119 HR 9084 RH: Department of Energy Nuclear Transparency Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr9084rh

    FAPD-AI: The reported bill, the Department of Energy Nuclear Transparency Act, requires the Secretary of Energy to post public announcements on a Department of Energy website within 72 hours of specified actions regarding covered DOE nuclear facilities of Hazard Category 1, 2, and 3. The required announcements cover alterations to directives and safety standards, issuance of preliminary documented safety analyses or documented safety analyses (which may be modified to remove commercially sensitive, classified, or controlled information), and agreements to authorize such facilities, including any applicable conditions. The bill also requires the Secretary to submit an annual report by January 31 to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources detailing authorization activities from the previous calendar year. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 00:01:27 Eastern time ET
    119 HR 9605 RH: Less Bureaucracy, Better Foreign Medical Accreditation Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr9605rh

    FAPD-AI: The reported bill, the Less Bureaucracy, Better Foreign Medical Accreditation Act, transfers from the Secretary of Education to the Secretary of Health and Human Services all functions related to the National Committee on Foreign Medical Education and Accreditation. The bill also transfers related personnel, assets, contracts, records, and unexpended appropriations, directs the Director of the Office of Management and Budget to ensure no net increase in full-time equivalent employees, and sets out savings, continuation of suits, and reference-substitution provisions. The transfer takes effect six months after enactment, with early implementation permitted, and the bill was committed to the Committee of the Whole House on November 5, 2026. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 00:01:27 Eastern time ET
    119 HR 9612 RH: American Enrichment Deployment Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr9612rh

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 9612, the American Enrichment Deployment Act, was introduced on July 9, 2026, referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and reported with an amendment on November 5, 2026 (Report No. 119-875). The bill amends Section 193 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 to permit construction of a uranium enrichment facility before a license is issued under sections 53 and 63, under the same terms applicable to other licensed fuel cycle facilities, while stating that this does not limit the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's authority to deny a license application. It directs the Commission to issue or revise implementing regulations within 180 days of enactment and provides that the National Environmental Policy Act, hearing rights under section 189, and Commission inspection authority are not affected. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 00:01:27 Eastern time ET
    119 HR 9613 RH: Nuclear Advisory Committee Reform Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr9613rh

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 9613, the Nuclear Advisory Committee Reform Act, was introduced on July 9, 2026 by Representative Harshbarger, referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and reported with an amendment on November 5, 2026 (Report No. 119-877). The bill amends Section 29 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 to set the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards at a maximum of 15 members appointed by the Commission, limit members to two four-year terms unless the Commission determines there is a compelling need for continued service, and specify the Committee's review duties and areas of focus. It also permits the Committee to decline review of certain license applications under section 182(b) and makes conforming amendments to sections 163 and 192 of the Act. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 00:01:27 Eastern time ET
    119 HR 9614 RH: NRC Staff Pay Alignment Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr9614rh

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 9614, the NRC Staff Pay Alignment Act, was introduced on July 9, 2026 by Representative Menendez, referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and committed to the Committee of the Whole House on November 5, 2026 (Report No. 119-876). The bill amends Section 161B of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 to authorize the Chairman to fix the compensation of career appointees at a rate not greater than 110 percent of the maximum basic pay for Senior Executive Service positions within the Commission. It also adds the number of career appointees with compensation fixed under this authority to the required reporting, and makes a conforming amendment to the Government Accountability Office report provision in section 502(b) of the ADVANCE Act of 2024. BILLS-SEL-01
